reveal.text: A singly linked list is `A → B → C → None`. Each node stores a value and a `next` reference. You already have `prev = A` and want to remove `victim = B` without losing `C`.
A singly linked list reaches each next item by following references. To remove a known node when its predecessor is known, make the predecessor point to the victim's successor.

cells.array: May need to shift later items

reveal.text: Linked lists fit workloads that already have node references and frequently rewire nearby links. They are a poor fit when fast random indexing is the main operation.
Before changing a link, know which node must remain reachable afterward.
To remove B from `A → B → C`, what should `A.next` become? Answer: `C`.

glossary.definition: A value plus a reference to another node.
The node immediately before another node.

reveal.text: Remove every `X` from `X → A → X → B → None`. The real head might need to be removed, which normally creates a special case.
A sentinel, or dummy head, is an extra non-data node placed before the real list. It gives the first real node a predecessor, so head deletion can use the same rewiring rule as other deletions.

items: Start: `D → X → A → X → B → None`

annotations.title: Create a predecessor for the head
annotations.explanation: The sentinel is not part of the logical data.

annotations.title: Return the real head
annotations.explanation: The real head may have changed during removals.

reveal.text: Use a sentinel when insertions or deletions at the logical head would otherwise need separate control flow.
The sentinel makes the head behave like an ordinary node with a predecessor.
After using a dummy head, which reference is the real list head? Answer: `dummy.next`.

reveal.text: Reverse `A → B → C → None` in place so the result is `C → B → A → None`. The main risk is losing the part of the list that has not been processed yet.
Reverse one link at a time. Before changing `current.next`, save the original next node so the remaining suffix stays reachable.

reveal.code:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    current = head
    while current:
        next_node = current.next
        current.next = prev
        prev = current
        current = next_node
    return prev

annotations.title: Save before rewiring
annotations.explanation: Without this reference, the unprocessed suffix could become unreachable.

annotations.title: Reverse one edge
annotations.explanation: Only after saving next do we point current backward.

reveal.text: Save `next`, reverse the link, then advance both pointers.
Which value must be saved before `current.next` is changed? Answer: `current.next`.

reveal.text: A parser reads `([{}])`. Every closing delimiter must match the most recently opened delimiter that has not been closed yet.
A stack is last in, first out (LIFO). Push new unresolved items on top; pop the newest item first.
Use a stack when the newest unresolved item must be handled next: nested delimiters, undo history, or depth-first work.
A queue removes the oldest waiting item first. That is the opposite order from a stack.
Newest item out first → stack.
Undo should remove the oldest edit or the newest edit? Answer: The newest edit.
Files A, B, and C are accepted in that order. A background uploader must process them in the same order they arrived.
A queue is first in, first out (FIFO). Add new work at the back and remove the oldest waiting work from the front.

reveal.code:
from collections import deque

jobs = deque()
jobs.append("A")
jobs.append("B")
first = jobs.popleft()

annotations.title: Add at the right
annotations.explanation: New work joins the back of the queue.

annotations.title: Remove from the left
annotations.explanation: The oldest queued item is processed first.

reveal.text: Python `deque` supports appends and pops from either end with approximately O(1) performance. Removing index 0 from a list requires O(n) memory movement.
Oldest item out first → queue.
For queued `[A, B, C]`, which item should be processed first? Answer: `A`.
For readings `[2, 1, 5, 3, 6]`, find the first later reading that is strictly larger for each position. Repeatedly scanning the remaining suffix would redo work.
A monotonic stack keeps unresolved positions in sorted value order. For next-greater problems, a decreasing stack lets a new larger value resolve smaller values at the top.

items: Read `1` → `1` is not greater than `2`; stack `[2, 1]`.
Read `6` → resolve `3` with `6`, then resolve `5` with `6`.

reveal.text: Use a monotonic stack when each item waits for the next or previous item that is larger or smaller, and unresolved candidates can be discarded once a better boundary arrives.
Keep only unresolved candidates that can still matter to a future value.
When reading `5` after stack values `[2, 1]`, which values are resolved? Answer: `1` and `2`.

reveal.text: A simulator receives future events continuously and repeatedly needs the event with the earliest timestamp. Example timestamps arrive as `20`, `5`, and `12`.
A priority queue returns the item with the best priority. A min-heap is one implementation: the smallest item is kept at the root, while the rest of the structure is only partially ordered.

items: The root is `5` because it is the smallest timestamp.
Pop `5`; the heap restores its invariant so the next smallest item becomes the root.

reveal.code:
import heapq

events = []
heapq.heappush(events, 20)
heapq.heappush(events, 5)
heapq.heappush(events, 12)
next_event = heapq.heappop(events)

annotations.title: Insert while keeping the heap invariant
annotations.explanation: The heap reorganizes only as much as needed.

annotations.title: Remove the smallest item
annotations.explanation: Python's `heapq` min-heap returns the smallest item.

reveal.text: Need the current minimum or maximum repeatedly while items change → consider a heap.
In Python's min-heap, which item is at `heap[0]`? Answer: The smallest item.

glossary.definition: A collection that returns the item with the best priority rather than the oldest item.
An ordering rule that keeps the best-priority item at the root.

reveal.text: Scores arrive as `[8, 3, 12, 5, 10]`. Keep only the `K = 3` largest scores without sorting every value.
For the K largest values, keep a min-heap of at most K items. Its root is the smallest value currently inside the top K, so the root acts as the cutoff.
Use a bounded heap when K is much smaller than the total number of items and only the top or bottom K matter.
For K largest values, the min-heap root is the current entry cutoff.
Current top-3 heap represents `{8, 10, 12}`. Should score `7` enter? Answer: No.
Three streams are already sorted: A=`[1, 4, 9]`, B=`[2, 6]`, C=`[3, 7]`. Produce one sorted output without loading and re-sorting every item together.
Because each stream is sorted, only its current front item can be the next global output. A min-heap can compare one frontier item from each stream.
Use k-way heap merge when several inputs are already sorted and should be streamed into one sorted output.
Keep one current frontier per sorted input; after popping one, advance only that input.
After popping a value from stream B, which stream supplies the replacement frontier? Answer: Stream B.
